title: Inside the Trade Show Where Companies Sell AI to the Police
hook: Facial-recognition cameras, 911 chatbots, gunshot-detection, and AI report-writing — a police-chiefs' tech conference showed how far AI has already moved into everyday policing.
key_points: A major US police-chiefs' technology conference in Fort Worth showcased AI tools aimed at police departments.
On the showroom floor: facial-recognition cameras, automated license-plate readers, and body cameras.
Also on offer: chatbots to field non-emergency 911 calls, gunshot-detection platforms, drones, and AI report-writing tools.
The pitch is automating routine work — but much of that 'routine' work sits inside the legal process itself.
Press were barred from entering; reporting relied on interviews with attendees outside the venue.
content_html: Facial recognition tends to dominate the conversation about AI and policing, but a recent police-chiefs' technology conference in Fort Worth, Texas made clear how much further it's already spread. The Verge's reporter — barred from entering the venue as press, and left to interview attendees outside — found a showroom stocked with far more than face-scanning cameras: automated license-plate readers, body cameras, chatbots built to field non-emergency 911 calls, gunshot-detection platforms, drones, and AI tools that write police reports.
extra_html: The sales pitch across all of it is familiar: automate the routine parts of the job so officers can focus elsewhere. The catch is that a lot of "routine" police work — how an incident gets described in a report, which calls get flagged for follow-up, which plate gets logged — sits directly inside the legal process that can lead to charges, warrants, or arrests. Handing pieces of that to AI doesn't just save time; it changes who (or what) is doing some of the earliest, most consequential steps in a case, often with little public visibility into how the tools actually make their calls. That opacity was compounded here by the conference itself being closed to press, a small irony given that the products being sold — surveillance and automated law-enforcement tools — are precisely the kind of technology whose use the public has the most reason to want visibility into.

related.title: Facial Recognition
related.hook: The same AI that unlocks your phone can pick your face out of a crowd. It's convenient at your fingertips and unsettling at a city's scale — and it makes mistakes, unevenly.

related.title: Rules & Regulation
related.hook: AI raced ahead of the law, and governments are now scrambling to catch up. The big debate: how to curb real harms without strangling a genuinely useful technology.
